blogPost.headline: Loitering detection: what it catches that motion does not

blogPost.headline: How many days of CCTV footage are you really keeping?

blogPost.headline: Face recognition at a badly lit gate

blogPost.headline: How many photos does face enrolment actually need

blogPost.headline: Can someone fool face attendance with a photo?

blogPost.headline: Attendance when your workforce triples for a season

blogPost.headline: Getting a new joiner onto attendance in five minutes

blogPost.headline: The five causes of every overtime dispute

blogPost.headline: Switching attendance systems without losing history

blogPost.headline: When an employee refuses biometric attendance

blogPost.headline: Attendance data: what to keep, what to delete, when
blogPost.description: Attendance retention isn't one number. The statutory register has a legal minimum keep period; the biometric template behind it doesn't, and should usually be deleted on exit. A practical schedule.

blogPost.headline: Field staff attendance: geofencing without micromanaging
blogPost.description: Geofencing can prove a service engineer reached the client site, or it can turn into tracking someone's lunch break. The difference is what you measure and what you tell them.

blogPost.headline: Fingerprint attendance systems: where they work, where they fail

blogPost.headline: Biometric attendance machine price in India: the full math

blogPost.headline: Leave, holidays and attendance: keeping one calendar

blogPost.headline: Rotating shifts and attendance: getting the rules right

blogPost.description: Proxy attendance survives fingerprint machines, cards and registers because all three record a credential, not a person. The four controls that actually work, ranked by how hard they are to defeat.

blogPost.headline: How many cameras does a warehouse actually need?

blogPost.headline: Your camera has been offline for weeks. Would you know?

blogPost.headline: CCTV AMC in India: what it should actually include

blogPost.headline: Connecting biometric attendance to payroll without retyping
blogPost.description: Most attendance errors are not scanning errors — they are introduced between the machine and the payslip, by a person with a spreadsheet. What a real payroll integration has to handle.

blogPost.headline: Attendance for contract labour: the compliance gap nobody plans for
blogPost.description: Contract workers rotate faster than any enrolment process, yet the principal employer often carries obligations for them. Where the record breaks, and how to close it without a week of admin.

blogPost.headline: Attendance records under Indian law: what you must keep
blogPost.description: Indian labour law requires employers to maintain attendance and wage registers — and the DPDP Act now governs the biometric data many employers use to produce them. A plain-language guide to both obligations.

blogPost.headline: AI CCTV or another security guard? An honest comparison

blogPost.headline: Why your CCTV alerts got muted, and how to earn them back
blogPost.description: Every site that muted its alerts did so for a good reason. The four causes of alert fatigue, and the tuning sequence that makes notifications worth reading again.

blogPost.headline: Aadhaar based attendance and AEBAS, explained plainly
blogPost.description: AEBAS is the government's Aadhaar-linked attendance system, and it is compulsory for some employers and unavailable to others. Here is who it actually applies to, and what private employers can use instead.

blogPost.headline: Can you add AI to CCTV cameras you already own?

blogPost.description: Fingerprint readers fail exactly where factories need them most. But face-based attendance has its own limits, and you should know both before switching.

blogPost.description: Traditional CCTV saves the footage after the damage is done. Proactive, AI-driven security detects, alerts and acts while there's still time to change the outcome.

mainEntity.name: How is AI intruder detection different from normal CCTV motion alerts?

acceptedAnswer.text: Motion alerts fire whenever pixels change, which includes rain, insects, shadows and headlights. AI intruder detection classifies the moving object first, so it only alerts you for a person or vehicle entering a zone you defined. In practice that is the difference between forty alerts a night and two.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to buy new AI CCTV cameras?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. PGAK works with your existing cameras as long as they expose an RTSP stream through the DVR or NVR, which nearly all modern systems do. The AI runs as software alongside them, so you keep the hardware you already paid for.

mainEntity.name: Does it work at night?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The model is trained on infrared and low-light footage, which is when most intrusions happen. Night performance depends on your cameras having usable IR illumination — something we check during the free camera audit.

mainEntity.name: Will it alert me for stray dogs or cats?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not unless you ask it to. Animals are classified separately from people and are suppressed by default — this is one of the biggest sources of false alarms in Indian installations, particularly at factory and warehouse perimeters.

mainEntity.name: What happens to my footage — is it sent to the cloud?

acceptedAnswer.text: Processing runs on an edge device at your site, so video stays on your premises by default. Only the small alert clips you choose to receive leave the building. See our privacy policy for the full detail.

mainEntity.name: Can people cheat face attendance the way they share fingerprints?

acceptedAnswer.text: Buddy punching is far harder, because the record stores the actual frame the recognition came from. If a mark is disputed you look at the photograph of who walked through, rather than trusting that the right finger was on the reader.

mainEntity.name: How much can false alerts actually be reduced?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sites typically see a 90%+ reduction after the first fortnight of tuning. The bigger change is qualitative: alerts go from something you swipe away to something you look at.

mainEntity.name: Why does my current system alert for shadows and rain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because conventional motion detection compares pixel changes between frames and has no concept of what an object is. Rain, shadows, headlights and swaying branches all change pixels. Object classification is a fundamentally different approach.

mainEntity.name: Could filtering cause me to miss a real intrusion?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's a real trade-off and we won't pretend otherwise. Filtering set too aggressively can suppress an ambiguous event. We start conservative, review the first weeks of events with you, and tighten only where the footage justifies it.

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if the threshold is set badly. Dwell times are per-zone — thirty seconds at a jewellery counter, three minutes at a fence — and staff are exempt. In practice the tuning takes a week and then the alerts become genuinely rare.

mainEntity.name: Is this the same as motion detection?

mainEntity.name: What should we do when a loitering alert fires?

acceptedAnswer.text: Look at the snapshot, and if it warrants it, have someone walk over. Presence is the deterrent. We'd caution against automated sirens on dwell alerts specifically — the false-positive cost is a confronted customer.

mainEntity.name: How many cameras does a jewellery shop need for good security?

acceptedAnswer.text: There's no fixed number — the count matters less than covering four specific positions: the counter (close enough to see hands and the display case), the strongroom or vault entry, the shop entrance, and the street outside. A shop with eight well-placed cameras at those points is better covered than one with twenty scattered ones.

mainEntity.name: What is distraction theft in a jewellery shop and how do cameras help?

acceptedAnswer.text: Distraction theft is when one person asks to see several items to occupy the staff member's attention while an accomplice pockets a piece or swaps it. A camera angled down onto the counter, close enough to see hands and tray contents rather than just faces, is what actually catches the swap — a wide entrance camera usually isn't close enough to help.

mainEntity.name: Can CCTV stop an armed robbery in a jewellery shop?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Cameras document an incident for identification and insurance; they don't physically stop someone who is already inside and armed. Preventing that relies on time-delay locks, a strongroom that isn't openable under duress alone, and a panic alarm that reaches help fast — cameras are the record, not the barrier.

mainEntity.name: How should a jewellery shop monitor staff without treating them as suspects?

acceptedAnswer.text: Through routine, applied-to-everyone reconciliation rather than watching any one person: stock counts against transaction records, and access logs on the strongroom that show who opened it and when. Framed as a standard control that protects honest staff by ruling them out quickly, not as surveillance aimed at anyone in particular, it settles disputes instead of creating them.

mainEntity.name: Does street-facing CCTV actually prevent jewellery shop robberies?

acceptedAnswer.text: It helps with the planning stage more than the act itself. Robberies are often preceded by someone loitering outside or walking past repeatedly over several days to study staff movements and locking routines. A camera covering the street and entrance can catch that pattern before the day of the robbery — but once someone is inside and committed, the camera's job shifts to identification, not prevention.

mainEntity.name: Can CCTV cameras help prevent spoilage in cold storage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, indirectly. A camera watching a cold room door can be paired with an analytics rule that flags the door being open beyond a set number of minutes, so someone is alerted before the temperature swing damages stock — the camera doesn't stop spoilage itself, it stops the delay in noticing.

mainEntity.name: What is a door-open dwell alert?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's a rule that measures how long a door stays open rather than just whether it opened. A forklift passing through for twenty seconds is normal; a door propped open for fifteen minutes during loading is a temperature event. Dwell time separates the two.

mainEntity.name: Do CCTV cameras work reliably inside cold storage rooms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard cameras struggle. Lens condensation and fogging are common when a camera moves between a warm anteroom and a sub-zero chamber, and connectors can become brittle in continuous cold. Cameras rated for the temperature range, mounted at the doorway rather than deep inside the chamber, hold up far better.

mainEntity.name: Is a door sensor better than a camera for tracking cold storage doors?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a simple open-or-shut signal, a magnetic door sensor is cheaper and more reliable than a camera, and it works in the dark. A camera earns its place when you also need to see who opened the door, whether product was carried out, or what was left leaning against it — evidence a sensor can't give you.

mainEntity.name: Should cold storage prioritise spoilage or theft when planning cameras?

acceptedAnswer.text: Spoilage first, in most cold stores. A single long door-open event can damage more stock value in an afternoon than a slow year of pilferage, and it happens far more often. Theft-focused placement still matters, but the door-dwell problem is usually the one nobody is currently measuring at all.

mainEntity.name: What should I do first after discovering a theft caught on CCTV?

acceptedAnswer.text: Export the relevant footage immediately, before doing anything else, onto a separate device — not just a phone video of the screen. Rolling storage overwrites on a fixed cycle, often just days, and a theft is frequently noticed after that cycle has already erased the recording you need.

mainEntity.name: How quickly does CCTV footage get overwritten?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends entirely on your storage capacity and camera count, but many small sites cycle through their full storage in under two weeks, and some in a matter of days. If you don't know your own retention window, treat every theft as urgent and export immediately rather than checking later.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to file an FIR to use CCTV footage for an insurance claim?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most insurance policies require a First Information Report for a theft claim, so filing one is usually a necessary step, not an optional one. File it as soon as practical after preserving the footage, since insurers typically want the FIR number as part of the claim documentation.

mainEntity.name: Can I just record my CCTV screen with my phone as evidence?

acceptedAnswer.text: It works as a last resort but it's the weakest form of evidence you can produce. A phone recording of a screen loses resolution, strips the recorder's original timestamp metadata, and is easy for the other side to challenge as unreliable. Always use the recorder's own export function when the recorder is still accessible.

mainEntity.name: Is CCTV in the workplace legal in India?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Employers can install CCTV in work areas — entrances, floors, warehouses, cash counters — for security, safety and operational reasons. What isn't automatically legal is where you point it and whether employees were told. mainEntity.name: Can an employer record inside a washroom or changing room?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Washrooms, changing rooms, prayer rooms and similar private spaces are not appropriate for CCTV coverage regardless of the stated reason, and doing so exposes the business to real legal risk. mainEntity.name: Do employees have to be told about workplace CCTV?

Visible signage at entrances and a short written note covering why cameras are there, what's recorded, who can view footage and how long it's kept satisfies both the spirit of India's data protection rules and basic fairness to staff.

mainEntity.name: How long can a company keep workplace CCTV footage?

acceptedAnswer.text: There's no single mandated number in India, so the practical rule is to keep footage only as long as its purpose requires, then delete it on a routine schedule — commonly 30 to 90 days for general monitoring, longer only for footage tied to an active investigation or dispute. Keeping everything indefinitely is itself a compliance risk under data minimisation principles.

mainEntity.name: Can CCTV footage be used to monitor employee performance?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can, but it should be disclosed as a purpose upfront rather than quietly repurposed later. Footage installed and announced as 'security' cameras being used months later for performance reviews or disciplinary action without prior notice is the kind of purpose creep that turns a defensible system into a legal liability.

Two things are needed first: create a Camera Account inside the Tapo app under Device Settings, Advanced Settings, Camera Account — this is a separate username and password from your TP-Link cloud login, and the cloud login will not work. mainEntity.name: Does AI CCTV work with Imou and Prama cameras?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prama we have tested directly, and it works. Imou we have not tested ourselves, but it is part of Dahua and uses the Dahua stream path, which is one of the paths a scan tries first — so it is expected to work in the same way. Prama is the Hikvision line in India and uses the Hikvision path. Both of those path families are tried early, so these cameras are normally found automatically once the recorder's IP address and login are entered.

If the manufacturer's app is the only way to see the video and there is no such setting, the camera is cloud-only and cannot be used by anything else.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to replace my cameras to add AI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. Analysis runs on the video stream a camera already produces, so if the camera can hand over an RTSP stream it can be used as it is, whatever its age or brand. acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, CCTV footage can be admitted as evidence in Indian courts, but electronic records need to satisfy specific legal requirements to be relied on — mainly proof that the recording is authentic and hasn't been altered. This is a general explanation, not legal advice; how a specific case is argued should be checked with a lawyer or compliance advisor.

mainEntity.name: What makes CCTV footage legally usable as evidence?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three things in practice: an intact, unedited original recording, a clear and accurate timestamp, and a documented chain of custody showing who accessed or copied the footage between the incident and its use in evidence. Missing any of the three gives the other side grounds to challenge it.

mainEntity.name: Does CCTV footage need a certificate to be used in court?

acceptedAnswer.text: Electronic evidence in India generally needs to be accompanied by a certificate confirming how the recording was produced and that it hasn't been tampered with, under the law governing electronic records. The exact format and how it's presented can vary by court and case, so this should be confirmed with a legal advisor before you need it.

mainEntity.name: How long should CCTV footage be kept for evidence purposes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Long enough to cover your normal retention window plus the time it typically takes to notice and report an incident — many disputes surface a week or more after the fact. If an incident is known, export and preserve that specific footage immediately, separately from your rolling storage, since normal retention will otherwise overwrite it.

mainEntity.name: What breaks the chain of custody for CCTV footage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Anything that leaves no record of who touched the footage: copying it to a personal phone instead of a logged export, editing or trimming the clip before saving it, or handling the original recorder without noting who accessed it and when. A copy nobody can account for is a copy that's easy to dispute.

mainEntity.name: What is loitering detection in CCTV?

acceptedAnswer.text: Loitering detection is a video analytics feature that measures how long a person or vehicle stays in a defined zone, and raises an alert once that dwell time crosses a threshold you set — for example, someone standing near a cash counter or a parked vehicle for more than two minutes. It is built on top of the same person-tracking that motion detection uses, with a timer added.

mainEntity.name: How is loitering detection different from motion detection?

acceptedAnswer.text: Motion detection alerts on any movement in frame — a person walking past counts the same as a person walking past ten times. Loitering detection tracks an individual across frames and only alerts once they've remained in a zone longer than the threshold, which filters out normal passing traffic and flags dwelling instead.

mainEntity.name: Where does loitering detection work best?

acceptedAnswer.text: Places where normal behaviour is brief and lingering is the anomaly: an ATM after hours, a back-gate blind spot, a parked-vehicle zone, or a counter area outside business hours. The clearer the line between 'passing through' and 'staying', the better the feature performs.

mainEntity.name: Can loitering detection cause false alarms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in any zone where lingering is normal — a bus stop, a smoking area, a queue, a reception bench. In those spots almost everyone crosses the dwell threshold, so the alert stops meaning anything and gets ignored, which defeats the purpose of having it.

mainEntity.name: Do all cameras need loitering detection turned on?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It's a zone-specific tool, not a blanket setting. Turning it on everywhere floods the same person who reviews alerts with noise from spots where dwelling is normal, and a flooded reviewer stops checking any of it.

mainEntity.name: What is ANPR (automatic number plate recognition)?

acceptedAnswer.text: ANPR is software that reads the characters on a vehicle's number plate from a camera image and turns them into text a computer can log, search or match against a list. It needs a plate that is sharp, roughly level, and large enough in the frame — everything after that depends on getting those three things right.

mainEntity.name: Does ANPR work reliably on Indian number plates?

acceptedAnswer.text: It works well at gates built for it — a fixed lane, correct camera height and angle, and good lighting. It struggles with the plate variation common in India: non-standard fonts, stickers, dirt, bent plates and multiple state formats. A camera aimed at general traffic rather than a controlled lane will read far fewer plates correctly than a vendor demo suggests.

mainEntity.name: Why does ANPR fail at some gates and not others?

acceptedAnswer.text: The four most common causes are a plate angle beyond about 30 degrees from straight-on, low light without a dedicated IR or white-light illuminator, vehicle speed that blurs the plate, and physical plate condition — mud, tint film, or a font that isn't the standard reflective one. Fix the angle and lighting first; they explain most failures.

mainEntity.name: Where should an ANPR camera be positioned?

acceptedAnswer.text: At a controlled point where vehicles slow down or stop — a boom barrier, a narrow gate, a toll-style lane — with the camera mounted to face the plate nearly head-on, at plate height, with its own lighting rather than relying on the site's general lighting. Open, multi-lane approaches with free-flowing traffic are the hardest place to make it work.

mainEntity.name: Can ANPR replace a security guard at the gate?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. ANPR logs and matches plates; it does not decide who to let in, inspect a vehicle, or handle a person on foot. It is a record-keeping and alerting tool that supports whoever is making the entry decision, not a replacement for them.

mainEntity.name: What CCTV problems does monsoon cause in India?

acceptedAnswer.text: The four repeat failures every monsoon are water entering through loose cable glands and open junction boxes, condensation fogging the inside of dome camera housings, corrosion at outdoor connectors that were never sealed, and power surges or outages during storms that reboot or damage recorders. The camera body itself is usually weather-rated and rarely the actual point of failure.

mainEntity.name: Why do camera lenses fog up in monsoon?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fogging happens when warm, humid air inside a housing meets a sudden drop in outside temperature during rain, and condenses on the inside of the dome or lens glass. It is a sealing problem, not a camera defect — a housing with a damaged gasket or a poorly closed cable entry lets humid air in continuously, so it fogs every time it rains rather than once.

mainEntity.name: Can a CCTV camera be permanently damaged by rain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if water reaches the electronics rather than staying on the outer shell. Most outdoor cameras are rated to shed rain hitting the housing, but water that enters through a cable gland, a cracked seal, or a joint left open during installation travels down the cable and can corrode the board inside, which is not repairable in the field.

mainEntity.name: What should be on a pre-monsoon CCTV checklist?

acceptedAnswer.text: Check every outdoor junction box and cable gland for a tight seal, inspect dome housings for cracked gaskets or trapped moisture, test earthing at the camera and at the DVR/NVR, confirm cable runs slope so water can't pool at a low point, and verify the UPS or inverter actually holds load for as long as your typical outage lasts.

mainEntity.name: Does a power backup matter for CCTV during monsoon?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — monsoon storms are when power cuts and voltage spikes both happen most often, and a recorder that reboots mid-storm can lose the exact window you needed footage from. A UPS sized for the cameras, the switch, and the recorder together, not just the recorder alone, is the part most sites get wrong.

mainEntity.name: What are CCTV camera blind spots?

acceptedAnswer.text: A blind spot is any area a person can stand, walk through, or work in that no camera actually covers clearly — not just areas with no camera at all, but also zones a nearby camera technically faces but can't resolve, because of distance, an obstruction, or a bad angle. Corners, gaps between two cameras' fields of view, and areas behind pillars or stacked stock are the most common ones.

mainEntity.name: How do thieves find blind spots in CCTV coverage?

acceptedAnswer.text: The same way a security consultant would: by watching the site from outside for a few minutes and noting where cameras are mounted, then walking the boundary looking for the gap between two camera views, a spot behind an obstruction, or an area lit poorly enough that footage would be useless even if a camera does cover it. This takes far less time than most owners assume.

mainEntity.name: Where are blind spots most commonly missed during CCTV installation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Corners of a compound wall, the side or rear of a building where cameras are added as an afterthought, areas behind parked vehicles or stacked material, staff entrances separate from the main gate, and any spot directly beneath a camera — a wide-angle lens mounted for distance coverage often has almost no useful view of the ground right under it.

mainEntity.name: How can I check my own site for blind spots without hiring a consultant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Walk the full perimeter from outside, at the pace and path an intruder would use, and at each point ask which camera would clearly identify someone here — not which camera is nearby, but which one would actually resolve a face or an action. Anywhere you can't name a camera confidently is a blind spot worth fixing.

mainEntity.name: Does adding more cameras fix blind spots?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if they're placed to close specific gaps found during a walk-around. Adding cameras without first identifying where the gaps are usually just adds more coverage to areas that were already covered, while the actual blind spots — corners, undersides, poorly lit stretches — stay exactly as exposed as before.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between IP and analogue CCTV cameras?

acceptedAnswer.text: IP cameras digitise video inside the camera and send it over a network cable (usually CAT6 with PoE for power). Analogue cameras send an unprocessed video signal down a coaxial cable to a DVR, which does the digitising centrally. IP typically gives higher resolution and easier scaling; analogue typically costs less and uses simpler, more forgiving cabling.

mainEntity.name: Is an IP camera better than an analogue camera?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not automatically. IP is usually the better choice for high resolution, long cable runs, or a site that will keep adding cameras over years. Analogue is often the better choice for a small, fixed site on a budget, or where the existing coaxial cabling is in good condition and rewiring would cost more than the cameras.

mainEntity.name: Can analogue cameras run AI analytics?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the DVR outputs a stream that analytics software can read, or with a small IP encoder added at the DVR. Analytics runs on the video stream, not on the camera type, so a well-maintained analogue system is not locked out of AI detection — it just needs that stream exposed.

mainEntity.name: Which is cheaper, IP or analogue CCTV, in India?

acceptedAnswer.text: Camera-for-camera, analogue hardware is usually cheaper, and coaxial cabling is more tolerant of amateur termination than CAT6 with PoE. IP can end up cheaper overall on a new, larger site because one network cable carries both power and data, cutting the cabling run in half. On a small site or a rewiring job, analogue is usually the lower total cost.

mainEntity.name: Should I upgrade my analogue CCTV system to IP?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if you have a specific reason: you need resolution your analogue system cannot deliver, you are adding many more cameras than your current cabling supports, or you are wiring a new site from scratch. Replacing a working analogue system for the sake of a newer label is rarely worth the cabling cost.

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The rule restricts what may be sold, imported and manufactured — not what is already installed and working. A camera bought and fitted before the deadline can keep running. mainEntity.name: What are Essential Requirements (ER) for CCTV cameras?

acceptedAnswer.text: They are baseline security conditions for the device itself. They cover secure firmware and a safe way to update it, encrypted communication so footage and credentials are not sent in the clear, proper authentication with no hardcoded or hidden default passwords, and protection against tampering at the hardware level. The intent is that a camera added to your network does not become the weakest point on it.

mainEntity.name: How do I check if a CCTV camera is STQC certified before buying?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ask the supplier for the documents, not a verbal assurance: the BIS registration under the Compulsory Registration Order and the STQC certificate covering the exact model you are being quoted. Check that the model number on the certificate matches the model on the quotation, because certification is issued per model and a nearby model in the same range is not covered by it. A brochure claim or a line in an email is not evidence.

acceptedAnswer.text: IP cameras need outdoor-rated CAT6 (or CAT5e at a push) carrying both data and power over PoE. Analogue cameras need coaxial cable rated for the resolution in use, plus a separate power run. Indoor-grade cable used outdoors is the single most common wrong choice — it cracks and lets in moisture within a year or two.

mainEntity.name: Does CCTV cabling need conduit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, for any run outdoors, on a roof, or exposed to sun. UV breaks down unprotected cable jacket in one or two seasons, and open cable is an easy target for rodents and monkeys. Conduit costs more upfront and is the first thing cut from a tight quote.

mainEntity.name: Why do CCTV cameras fail after a year even though the hardware is fine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most 'camera failures' in year two are cabling failures. A joint with no waterproof gel corrodes after a monsoon, a badly terminated connector adds resistance that fails intermittently, or the cable itself has degraded from UV exposure. Swapping the camera fixes nothing because the camera was never the problem.

mainEntity.name: What is a PoE budget and why does it matter for CCTV?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is the total wattage a PoE switch can deliver across all connected cameras. Each camera draws more when its IR illuminator or heater is running, typically at night or in winter. A switch sized for daytime draw silently drops or reboots cameras once several run their heaters together — which is exactly when you need footage most.

mainEntity.name: Can AI analytics be added to a badly cabled system?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not reliably. Analytics depends on a stable, unbroken video stream. A camera that drops out for a few seconds an hour will generate false alerts or miss events entirely, no matter how good the software is. Cabling has to be fixed before analytics is worth adding.

acceptedAnswer.text: Look at the cable running from your camera to the box. A single round coaxial cable (often with a separate thin power cable) means DVR and an analogue camera. mainEntity.name: Can AI video analytics work with a DVR?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sometimes. It depends on whether the DVR can output an RTSP stream — a standard way of sharing live video over a network — which most DVRs from the last five to six years can, usually via the manufacturer's software or a small settings change. If it cannot, the practical fix is adding one IP camera at the position that needs analytics rather than replacing the whole system.

mainEntity.name: Should I replace my DVR with an NVR?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not automatically. If your analogue cameras still produce a usable, sharp image at the distance you need, a wholesale swap is often an unnecessary expense. Replacement earns its cost when you specifically need higher resolution at long range, face-level detail at a gate, or you are wiring a new site from scratch anyway.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate CCTV storage days?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide your recorder's total storage capacity in gigabytes by the total daily storage used across all cameras. Daily use per camera depends on resolution, frame rate, compression and how much motion the scene has, so the only reliable way to know it is to check the recorder's own storage statistics rather than estimate from a spec sheet.

mainEntity.name: Why does CCTV retention shrink over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Storage is fixed at installation, but cameras usually get added afterward — a new gate, a new aisle, a new floor — without anyone adding storage to match. Every additional camera divides the same disk among more feeds, so retention falls silently unless someone recalculates it.

mainEntity.name: What affects how much storage a camera uses per day?

acceptedAnswer.text: Four things: resolution (more pixels means more data), frame rate (more frames per second means more data), compression standard (H.265 uses roughly half the storage of H.264 for the same picture), and scene activity, because most recorders only write footage when motion is detected, so a quiet back office uses far less than a busy loading bay.

mainEntity.name: How many days of CCTV footage should a business keep?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single correct number — it depends on how quickly a business would need to review a past incident, and this varies by state and by the rules that apply to a given premises. Fifteen to thirty days is a common practical target for a small business; verify against your own sector's requirements rather than assuming a default is enough.

mainEntity.name: Does face recognition work in low light?

acceptedAnswer.text: Poorly, and it is worth separating two different jobs. Detecting that a person is present works fine in low light because infrared sensors are built for exactly that. Identifying which specific person it is needs far more detail — skin tone, contrast and fine facial features — which infrared footage does not preserve well. That is why a gate camera can 'see' someone perfectly at night and still fail to recognise them.

mainEntity.name: Can infrared cameras be used for face recognition?

acceptedAnswer.text: Infrared is excellent for detecting movement and presence in the dark, but it flattens the contrast a face-matching algorithm depends on. Faces come out as pale, similar-looking ovals with washed-out detail, which is why IR-only footage is reliable for motion and person detection but weak for identification.

mainEntity.name: What is the cheapest fix for face recognition at a dark gate?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases, one warm-white light aimed correctly at the point where people's faces pass, not a new camera. A camera upgrade to a low-light-optimised sensor can cost many times more than a single fixture, and often solves less of the problem if the light hitting the face is still wrong.

mainEntity.name: Where should gate lighting be placed for face recognition to work?

acceptedAnswer.text: In front of or beside the walking path, angled onto the face, and away from the lens. Light placed behind the person creates a silhouette the camera cannot read. Light aimed straight into the lens causes glare and washes out the very detail you need.

mainEntity.name: Will better lighting guarantee face recognition works at night?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Lighting fixes the most common night-time failure, but a camera mounted too high, a subject looking away, or fast walking through the frame will still cause misses. Lighting removes one large obstacle, not every obstacle.

mainEntity.name: Does more megapixels mean I can identify faces further away?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not on its own. Megapixels tell you the total detail a sensor captures across its whole field of view. If that field of view is wide, the same pixels get spread thin over a large area, so a high-megapixel camera with a wide lens can still show a face as a handful of blurry pixels at distance. What matters is pixels per metre at the exact spot the face appears, not the megapixel number on the box.

mainEntity.name: Why does a 4MP camera fail to identify a face at 40 metres?

acceptedAnswer.text: With a typical wide lens, a 4MP camera's roughly 2,688 horizontal pixels can be spread across a view that is 60-70 metres wide at 40 metres' distance — around 40 pixels per metre. Identifying a stranger reliably generally needs well over 100 pixels per metre. At 40 pixels per metre, a face occupies only a few pixels across, which is not enough detail for a human reviewer or software to identify anyone.

mainEntity.name: What is pixels per metre and why does it matter more than megapixels?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pixels per metre is the camera's horizontal pixel count divided by how wide its field of view is at a given distance. It tells you how much detail actually lands on a person standing at that spot, which is the number that determines whether a face, a plate or a badge is readable — not the total megapixel count printed on the camera.

mainEntity.name: How can I get better identification range without buying a new camera?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fit a narrower lens (a longer focal length or a varifocal set to zoom in) on the same camera. Narrowing the field of view concentrates the same pixel count onto a smaller area, raising pixel density at distance — at the cost of covering less width, so you may need an extra camera to keep the rest of the area covered.

acceptedAnswer.text: Not if the system has liveness detection, which is now standard in most face attendance products. Liveness checks look for signs of a live, three-dimensional person — subtle movement, depth, sometimes a prompted blink or head turn — and reject a flat printed photo or a phone screen held up to the camera because those don't move or reflect light the way a real face does.

mainEntity.name: What is liveness detection in face recognition?

acceptedAnswer.text: Liveness detection is a check that runs alongside face matching to confirm the camera is looking at an actual live person, not a photo, video replay, or mask. It works by analysing depth, texture, and small natural movements that a flat image or screen cannot reproduce.

mainEntity.name: What can still defeat face recognition liveness detection?

acceptedAnswer.text: High-quality liveness detection is genuinely hard to spoof with a printed photo or phone screen, but no system is unbeatable in principle — a very high-resolution video replay, a 3D-printed mask, or a determined attacker with specialist equipment can, in theory, challenge weaker implementations. mainEntity.name: Does face recognition work for employees wearing turbans?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in almost all cases. A turban covers the hair and scalp, not the facial landmarks — eyes, nose, mouth, jawline — that face recognition actually measures. acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, as long as the helmet does not have a visor or chin strap covering the lower face. A standard hard hat leaves the whole face exposed and does not affect recognition. mainEntity.name: Can face recognition work through a surgical or dust mask?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is the one covering that genuinely defeats most systems. A mask hides the nose, mouth and jawline, which are core landmarks for measurement, and accuracy drops sharply. mainEntity.name: Do sunglasses or scarves stop face recognition from working?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sunglasses hide the eyes, which are among the most important landmarks, and usually cause a failed match. A scarf worn loosely around the neck has no effect, but pulled up over the nose and mouth it behaves the same as a mask. The rule is simple: whatever covers the eyes, nose or mouth is the problem.

mainEntity.name: What affects face recognition accuracy the most?

acceptedAnswer.text: Four things in practice: how many pixels sit between the eyes in the camera frame, the angle of the face to the lens, the lighting at the point of capture, and how much motion blur is in the frame. A face recognition system that is strong on paper still misses people if any one of these is wrong at your actual gate.

mainEntity.name: How many pixels between the eyes does face recognition need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most face recognition engines want at least 40 to 60 pixels between the eyes to identify a person reliably, and quality drops sharply below that. This is a function of camera resolution, lens choice and distance from the gate, not of the software's advertised accuracy.

mainEntity.name: Does camera angle affect face recognition accuracy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, significantly. A camera looking down at a steep angle, or mounted to the side of where people actually walk, captures a distorted or partial view of the face. Accuracy claims are almost always measured on a face looking near-straight at the lens, which a badly aimed gate camera rarely produces.

mainEntity.name: Can face recognition work in low light or with motion blur?

acceptedAnswer.text: Low light and motion blur are two of the most common reasons recognition fails on site. Poor lighting starves the camera of the detail it needs, and a fast walking pace under a slow shutter speed smears the face across several pixels. Both are usually fixable with a lamp or a shutter-speed setting, not a different algorithm.

mainEntity.name: Is a vendor's stated accuracy percentage reliable?

acceptedAnswer.text: Treat it as a lab number, not a promise for your gate. It was almost certainly measured on well-lit, front-facing, high-resolution images — conditions your actual entrance may not match. What matters is accuracy at your specific camera, angle and lighting, which no brochure number can tell you.

mainEntity.name: What is a good grace period for a late mark policy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most Indian factories and offices settle somewhere between five and fifteen minutes, timed from the official shift start rather than from the first punch of the day. The exact number matters less than picking one, writing it down, and applying it the same way to everyone — an unpublished or unevenly enforced grace period causes more arguments than a strict published one.

mainEntity.name: Should every late mark cost the same, or should it escalate?

acceptedAnswer.text: A flat penalty on the first late mark of the month feels harsh, and no penalty until the fifth feels like there's no policy at all. Most workable policies escalate: a warning for the first one or two late marks, then a defined deduction from the third, reset each month. Escalation gives people room for a genuine one-off without removing the consequence for a pattern.

mainEntity.name: What should happen when a biometric scanner or network failure causes a false late mark?

acceptedAnswer.text: The policy needs a named exception path before it needs anything else: a supervisor who can log the failure, a short window to raise it, and a correction that appears on the same day's record. Without this path, every device failure becomes a dispute, and workers start treating the machine as adversarial rather than neutral.

mainEntity.name: Does photo or video evidence help settle late-mark disputes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — a timestamped photo or video frame at the point of entry settles a disputed late mark in seconds, because both sides are looking at the same evidence instead of arguing about whose clock is right. It does not replace a written policy; it just removes the argument about what actually happened.

Three hundred workers arriving over two days can overwhelm enrolment even on a system that has plenty of room to store their records.

acceptedAnswer.text: Enrol at the gate on day one rather than in a back office later, keep the enrolment record minimal but complete enough to reconcile pay, and plan the exit the same way you planned the entry — a workforce that triples for a season also needs to shrink back cleanly, with old records archived rather than left active and unmonitored.

mainEntity.name: Does face recognition work for short-term or seasonal labour?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can, but enrolment quality matters more for short-term workers than for permanent staff, because there's no second attempt after a bad first photo — the person may be gone by the time the problem is noticed. mainEntity.name: Should seasonal workers be enrolled on paper first and entered into the system later?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's tempting when the queue is long, but reconciling paper attendance against a digital system after the fact is where most disputes and payroll errors originate. It's usually better to slow the gate down and enrol properly than to catch up afterward against records nobody can fully verify.

mainEntity.name: What is the biggest problem with a 3 shift attendance system?

acceptedAnswer.text: Midnight attribution. When a shift crosses midnight, the clock resets to a new calendar day mid-shift, and most systems attribute hours to whichever date the punch timestamp falls on rather than the shift the worker was actually on. This splits one continuous shift into two partial days on the report, which then disagrees with the payroll register.

mainEntity.name: Why do exit punches matter in a continuous operation?

acceptedAnswer.text: An entry-only system can tell you who arrived but not who is still on site, who left early, or who never left after their shift ended. In a 24x7 operation the next shift is arriving while the last one should be leaving, so without an exit event you cannot tell handover from overstay, and you cannot compute actual hours worked at all — only hours since the last punch.

mainEntity.name: How should shift handover overlap be handled in attendance software?

acceptedAnswer.text: Define the overlap as a named window, not a gap in the rules. If your shifts hand over for 15 minutes so the outgoing operator can brief the incoming one, both people being logged at the gate during that window is correct, not an anomaly. A system that flags every overlap as a duplicate or an error will train supervisors to ignore its alerts entirely.

mainEntity.name: Does face recognition work for night shift attendance?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can, but only if the camera and lighting at the gate were set up for night conditions specifically — good IR-lit face recognition at 2 a.m. is a different setup than good recognition in daylight, not the same camera doing double duty. A gate that recognises faces perfectly on the day shift and fails on the night shift usually has a lighting problem, not a software one.

mainEntity.name: What causes most overtime disputes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Nearly every overtime dispute traces back to one of five causes: rounding rules that shave minutes off real work, confusion between shift-end time and actual clock-out time, wrong rates on weekly-off or holiday overtime, missed punch-outs that get guessed at, and overtime worked without prior approval. Fixing the record-keeping around each one removes the argument, because there is no longer a fact in dispute.

mainEntity.name: How does rounding affect overtime pay?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rounding rules — for example, rounding every punch to the nearest 15 minutes — save a few minutes here and there that add up over a month. Workers notice the pattern even when management doesn't. The fix is to round consistently in both directions, or not round at all and let the system calculate to the minute.

mainEntity.name: What happens if an employee forgets to punch out?

acceptedAnswer.text: Without a record, someone has to guess the end time — usually the shift's scheduled end, which may be wrong in either direction. A missed punch-out should be flagged as an exception immediately, not discovered at month-end, so it can be corrected from a real signal like a gate camera or a supervisor's confirmation while everyone still remembers the shift.

mainEntity.name: Should unapproved overtime be paid?

acceptedAnswer.text: That's a policy decision, not a system one — but the policy has to be written down and applied the same way every time. The dispute isn't usually about whether unapproved hours get paid; it's about workers finding out the rule mid-argument instead of before they stayed late.

mainEntity.name: Why do weekly-off and holiday overtime rates cause disputes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the multiplier is easy to get wrong by hand and hard to verify without the raw data. A worker who worked a weekly-off shift wants to see the day marked correctly and the rate applied automatically, not recalculated manually by whoever is doing payroll that week.

mainEntity.name: How do I migrate to a new attendance system without losing history?

acceptedAnswer.text: Export your existing records in a plain, dated format before you touch anything — CSV with one row per punch, not a summarised monthly report. Run the old and new systems in parallel for at least one full pay cycle so you can compare them directly. Keep the old system's raw exports permanently, even after cutover, because a new vendor will migrate the summary but rarely the underlying punch-level data.

mainEntity.name: What attendance history actually transfers to a new system?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually the monthly summary — total present days, total absences, total overtime — transfers cleanly because it's just numbers. What rarely transfers is the punch-level detail: individual clock-in and clock-out times, manual-entry flags, and any photo or biometric evidence tied to a specific day. If you might need to dispute or verify an old record later, export that detail yourself before switching.

mainEntity.name: What export format should I ask my current vendor for?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ask for raw CSV or Excel with one row per attendance event — employee ID, date, time, device or camera ID, and entry type. Refuse a PDF-only export or a system that only offers pre-summarised monthly reports; both are useless if you ever need to answer a specific question about a specific day six months later.

mainEntity.name: Why shouldn't I cut over attendance systems at month-end?

acceptedAnswer.text: Month-end is when payroll is calculated from the attendance data, and a partial data set split across two systems makes every calculation a manual reconciliation. Cut over in the first or second week of a month instead, so the entire pay cycle that matters for the next payroll run sits inside one system, not divided across two.

mainEntity.name: How long should I run two attendance systems in parallel?

acceptedAnswer.text: One full pay cycle at minimum — typically a month. Parallel running is the only way to catch a mismatch, like a device miscounting shifts or a rule interpreting weekly-offs differently, before it reaches payroll. Running both costs a bit of double data entry for a few weeks; skipping it costs a disputed payroll run.

mainEntity.name: Can an employee legally refuse biometric attendance in India?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Biometric data is personal data under the DPDP Act, 2023, and collecting it needs informed consent. An employee can decline, and an employer cannot make biometric enrolment the only way to be marked present — a lawful non-biometric fallback has to exist.

mainEntity.name: Can a company fire or discipline someone for refusing biometrics?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not for the refusal itself. Disciplinary action has to rest on actual absence or lateness recorded through the fallback method, not on declining to enrol. Treat the refusal as a process question, not a conduct issue.

mainEntity.name: What is a lawful fallback for biometric attendance?

acceptedAnswer.text: A card, a PIN-based entry, or a manual register entry backed by a supervisor's sign-off — any method that records presence without capturing a fingerprint or face template. It should log the same fields (name, time, location) as the biometric system so reports stay consistent.

mainEntity.name: Does DPDP consent apply to face recognition on CCTV as well as fingerprints?

acceptedAnswer.text: It applies wherever the system creates and stores a biometric template tied to an identified person for a purpose like attendance. General CCTV recording for security is treated differently from enrolling someone's face as an attendance credential — the enrolment step is where consent matters most.

mainEntity.name: How long should attendance data be retained in India?

acceptedAnswer.text: There isn't a single answer — it depends on which record you mean. The statutory attendance register required under labour law typically has a minimum retention period set by state rules, often several years. The biometric template used to capture that attendance is a different kind of data and should usually be deleted much sooner, typically on the employee's exit.

mainEntity.name: Should biometric templates be deleted when an employee leaves?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in most cases. Once someone leaves, there's no ongoing purpose for their fingerprint or face template, and the DPDP Act requires personal data to be deleted once its purpose is served unless another law specifically requires keeping it. The attendance summary derived from it can be retained separately without keeping the biometric itself.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between the attendance register and the biometric template?

acceptedAnswer.text: The register is the output — dates, times, present/absent status — used for payroll and statutory compliance, and labour law often requires keeping it for years. The template is the input — a mathematical representation of a fingerprint or face used to identify the person — and has no independent legal retention requirement once matching is no longer needed.

mainEntity.name: Do CCTV attendance photos need to be deleted too?

acceptedAnswer.text: The enrolment photo or template used for matching should follow the same exit-triggered deletion as any other biometric. Raw security footage from cameras is usually governed by a separate, shorter retention window tied to storage capacity and security policy, not attendance rules.

mainEntity.name: Where does geofencing attendance not work well?

acceptedAnswer.text: Manual work wears down fingerprint ridges. acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not on its own. acceptedAnswer.text: Face recognition — either as a wall terminal, or as software on the CCTV cameras already at your entrances. Camera-based recognition removes the queue and the per-door hardware entirely: people are logged at walking pace and every record carries the photo it came from.

mainEntity.name: What is AEBAS?

acceptedAnswer.text: AEBAS stands for Aadhaar Enabled Biometric Attendance System. It is the Government of India's attendance platform, in which an employee enters their Aadhaar number or employee ID at a terminal and authenticates with a fingerprint or iris scan against the UIDAI database. It is used across central and many state government offices.

mainEntity.name: Can a private company use Aadhaar based attendance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Generally no, not in the AEBAS sense. Aadhaar authentication against the UIDAI database is restricted to entities permitted under the Aadhaar Act, which does not extend to an ordinary private employer wanting to track staff attendance. Private employers use their own biometric or face recognition systems instead, holding their own enrolment data.

mainEntity.name: Who is required to use AEBAS?

acceptedAnswer.text: AEBAS was rolled out for central government departments and their attached and subordinate offices, along with autonomous bodies, and several state governments have adopted it for their own departments. Whether it is mandatory for a particular office is decided by that department's own orders, not by a single national rule, so a government employee should check their department's circular rather than assume.

mainEntity.name: Why can't a private employer authenticate an employee's Aadhaar?

acceptedAnswer.text: Section 57 of the Aadhaar Act once allowed private bodies to seek Aadhaar authentication under a contract. The Supreme Court struck that down in its September 2018 Aadhaar judgment. The 2019 amendment to the Act created a narrow replacement route, but it requires UIDAI to approve the entity and requires the purpose to be backed by a law of Parliament or notified by the Central Government. Marking staff attendance is neither.

mainEntity.name: Is it legal to store an employee's Aadhaar number in an attendance system?

acceptedAnswer.text: Storing an Aadhaar number as a reference field is a different thing from authenticating against UIDAI, and it is not what AEBAS does. It is also not risk-free: an Aadhaar number is personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and collecting one you do not actually need creates an obligation without giving you an attendance benefit. Most employers are better off using their own employee code.

mainEntity.name: What can a private employer use instead of AEBAS?

acceptedAnswer.text: A self-contained attendance system where the employer enrols staff themselves. That is either a conventional fingerprint or card reader, or face recognition running on the entrance cameras the site already has. In both cases the biometric template belongs to the employer and is governed by the DPDP Act, with no connection to UIDAI.

mainEntity.name: Is CCTV legal in workplaces in India?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Indian employers routinely and lawfully operate CCTV in entries and exits, production and loading areas, parking, cash counters, stores and server rooms. The recognised limits are that cameras must not cover places where people have a reasonable expectation of privacy — washrooms and changing rooms in particular — and that covert audio recording is treated far more strictly than video. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 does not ban workplace CCTV; it governs how the resulting personal data is handled.

mainEntity.name: Do I need employee consent for face recognition attendance in India?

acceptedAnswer.text: You need, at minimum, clear notice of what is collected and why, and a defined and proportionate purpose. Whether signed consent is strictly required depends on which basis you rely on under the DPDP Act, 2023 — the Act contains a legitimate-uses provision covering employment purposes that many summaries overlook. The safe operating posture, and the one we build for, is enrolled-only and consent-based: nobody is in the face database unless they were enrolled deliberately and told why. Confirm your specific basis with your own legal counsel.

mainEntity.name: Can AI CCTV recognise people who are not employees?

acceptedAnswer.text: It should not identify them. A well-configured system holds face templates only for people who were deliberately enrolled — typically staff and contractors who were told. Everyone else is handled as an unidentified person: the system can register that a person is present, or that someone unknown is in a restricted area at an odd hour, without ever attaching a name. That distinction between detecting a person and identifying a person is the centre of the whole compliance question.

mainEntity.name: Is audio recording on CCTV legal in India?

acceptedAnswer.text: Audio is treated much more strictly than video, and covert recording of conversations carries risks that ordinary video surveillance does not. Most workplace deployments deliberately leave audio off. If you are considering recording sound, take specific legal advice first rather than treating it as a camera setting.

mainEntity.name: Does AI CCTV work without internet?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends entirely on where the analysis happens. If detection runs on a device installed at your site, the cameras keep recording and the AI keeps detecting through an internet outage — what pauses is delivery of alerts to your phone, which resumes when the link returns. If the system sends video to a cloud service to be analysed, detection itself stops when the connection does. Ask any vendor which of the two they are selling before you compare prices.

mainEntity.name: What happens to AI CCTV during a power cut?

acceptedAnswer.text: Power is the real single point of failure, not internet. Cameras, the DVR and the on-site processing device all need power, so an outage stops everything regardless of how clever the software is. This is why sites that care put the cameras, the recorder and the edge device on the same UPS or inverter circuit — a modest UPS covers the whole chain, because these are low-draw devices compared with lighting or machinery.

mainEntity.name: How much internet bandwidth does AI CCTV need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Far less than people expect, if the processing is local. When video is analysed on site, only events and short clips travel out, so a basic broadband line is usually sufficient and idle usage is very small. Cloud-analysed systems are the opposite: they must ship continuous video off site for every camera, which is why they are expensive to run on Indian links and why they fail hardest when the connection is unstable.

mainEntity.name: Will I know if my CCTV goes offline?

acceptedAnswer.text: You should, and this is worth testing before you buy. A system watching camera health can flag a camera that has stopped producing frames within about three minutes, and can flag a whole site whose on-site device has stopped checking in within about two. Many installations have no such warning at all, which is how sites discover a camera died six weeks ago only when they go looking for footage.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between AI CCTV and normal CCTV?

acceptedAnswer.text: Normal CCTV records so you can review footage after an incident. AI CCTV watches the same footage continuously and raises an alert while something is happening. The cameras, cabling and recorder are typically identical — the difference is software that understands what is in the frame, so the system can distinguish a person entering a restricted area from a dog, a shadow or a swaying branch, and tell somebody about it at the time rather than leaving it for you to find later.

mainEntity.name: Is AI CCTV better than normal CCTV?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is better at one specific thing: telling you at the time. If your problem is that incidents are discovered hours or days later, AI addresses that directly. If your problem is that you have no cameras covering the loading bay, or that the footage is too dark to be useful, AI does not fix either — you need coverage and lighting first. Buy it for the alerting, not as a general upgrade.

mainEntity.name: Can normal CCTV be upgraded to AI CCTV?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases yes, without replacing cameras. AI analytics read the video stream your existing DVR or NVR already produces, so a working estate of ordinary IP or HD-over-coax cameras can usually be reused as-is. Face recognition and number-plate reading are the two capabilities that often need a camera repositioned or added, because they must resolve something small and specific.

mainEntity.name: Does AI CCTV reduce false alarms?

acceptedAnswer.text: That is one of its main purposes. Conventional motion detection triggers on pixel change, which means headlights, rain, insects near the lens, shadows and moving foliage all generate alerts. Detection models classify what is actually in the frame, so a system can be set to raise an alert for a person in a restricted zone and to stay quiet for everything else. The practical result is a smaller number of alerts that are worth looking at.

mainEntity.name: What is CCTV tampering detection?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is the system watching its own cameras for signs of interference rather than watching for people. A lens being covered or sprayed, a camera being twisted away from what it was pointed at, or the view going suddenly dark are all detectable from the video itself, because each produces a distinctive change across the whole frame. Separately, a camera that stops sending frames altogether — unplugged, cable cut, or the recorder removed — can be detected by its absence.

mainEntity.name: How quickly can you tell if a CCTV camera has been disabled?

acceptedAnswer.text: A camera that has stopped producing frames can be flagged in about three minutes, and a whole site whose on-site device has stopped reporting in about two. Without that kind of monitoring, most sites find out days or weeks later, at the moment they go looking for footage of an incident and discover the camera had been dead the whole time.

mainEntity.name: What happens if thieves take the DVR?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the recording is only on that box, it leaves with the box, which is why recorders are targeted. The protection is that events and clips are copied off site as they happen, so what has already been sent is beyond reach of anyone in the building. A recorder being removed also stops all its cameras at once, which is itself a strong and immediate signal that something is wrong.

mainEntity.name: Can CCTV detect if a camera is moved or covered?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Covering a lens, spraying it, or turning a camera towards a wall or the ceiling each change the entire frame in a way that is straightforward to recognise, and can raise an alert at the time. This matters because these actions almost always happen before the thing you actually wanted the camera to record.

mainEntity.name: How many CCTV cameras does a warehouse need?

acceptedAnswer.text: It follows from entry points and value concentration rather than floor area. A typical mid-sized warehouse needs one camera per external door and shutter, one per loading bay, two to four covering the perimeter, one on the despatch and returns desk, one over any high-value or bonded storage, and wide coverage of the main floor. That usually lands between 12 and 30 cameras. Two warehouses of identical size can legitimately differ by double if one has four shutters and the other has one.

mainEntity.name: How do I decide where to put CCTV cameras in a factory?

acceptedAnswer.text: Work backwards from events rather than forwards from floor plans. Write down the specific things you want to be told about — someone entering the yard after hours, a shutter opening out of shift, stock leaving through despatch unrecorded — and for each one identify the spot where it becomes visible. That gives you positions with a defined job. Cameras placed to cover area, rather than to catch a defined event, are the ones that turn out to be useless on the day something happens.

mainEntity.name: Is it better to have more cameras or better cameras?

acceptedAnswer.text: Better placement beats both. A modest camera at head height beside a gate is more useful than an expensive one on a high mast covering the whole yard, because what matters is how many pixels land on the subject at the distance it actually appears. Once placement is right, resolution matters — but adding cameras to a badly planned layout mostly adds more views of nothing in particular.

mainEntity.name: How many cameras can one person monitor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Realistically, very few, and not for long. Attention degrades within minutes on a multi-camera wall, which is why live monitoring is the least reliable part of most installations. This is the reason detection is worth automating: the cameras are not the bottleneck and never were — the watching is.

mainEntity.name: Is face recognition attendance better than a biometric machine?

acceptedAnswer.text: For industrial gates where many people arrive at once, usually yes: there is no queue, no contact, and no PIN fallback for buddy punching. For a small air-conditioned office with ten staff, a fingerprint machine is often fine. The honest test is to run both for a fortnight and compare the records.

mainEntity.name: Does face recognition attendance work with helmets or masks?

acceptedAnswer.text: Partially. A face more than about 60° off-axis, heavily backlit, or covered by a mask or full helmet will be detected as a person but may not be identified. The practical fix is placing the attendance camera at the point where people naturally uncover — before the helmet zone — rather than fighting the covering.

mainEntity.name: How much does face recognition attendance cost compared to a biometric machine?

acceptedAnswer.text: A biometric machine costs roughly ₹8,000–₹25,000 up front plus AMC and replacements, per gate. Camera-based attendance with PGAK is billed per camera per month running on the gate camera you already own, with no per-employee charge, and one gate camera typically covers 150–250 employees — so most factories in India pay less than they were spending maintaining the machines.
